chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from one of our companions, from Abbad ibn Yaqoub al-Rawajini, from Saeed ibn Abd al-Rahman, who said:

I was with Musa ibn Abd Allah in Yanbu, and my travel expenses had run out during one of the journeys. So one of the sons of Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said to me, 'Who do you hope for (to intercede) for what has befallen you?' I said, 'Musa ibn Abd Allah.' He said, 'Then your need will not be fulfilled, and your seeking will not be accomplished.' I said, 'And why is that?' He said, 'Because I have found in some of the books of my forefathers (peace be upon him) that Allah (Exalted and Majestic) says...' and he mentioned something similar. I said, 'O son of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family)! Dictate it to me.' So he dictated it to me. I said, 'No, by Allah! I will not ask him for a need after it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the significance of delegating matters to Allah in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the nuanced Shia understanding of *tawakkul* by linking reliance on the Imam to specific divine promises recorded in their inherited books. The companion’s hesitation suggests that true success in delegating matters to Allah requires aligning one's supplication with the precise spiritual authority and scriptural evidence endorsed by the Ahl al-Bayt, rather than mere general trust. This underscores the Imam's role as the living interpreter of Quranic verses, ensuring that reliance is not just emotional but rooted in revealed truth.
